text: Hello and welcome to another episode of This is My Architecture. My name is Gaurav,
we're shooting from Mumbai. Today I've got Ranvijay with me from Haptic. Welcome, Ranvijay.
Thank you for having me, Gaurav.
And can you tell us what Haptic does as an organization and the role that you play?
So I currently head the DevOps practices at Haptic and I also take care of the systems
and applications architecture. Haptic is one of the largest conversational AI platforms
and we solve key problems of businesses using bots. These bots are spanned both over voice
and chat. The best part about building bots at Haptic is we can deploy these bots on multiple
channels, be it mobile apps, websites, voice assistants like Alexa, Google Assistant and
also multiple messaging platforms like Facebook, Twitter and recently we've also integrated
with WhatsApp. So we are offering our bots on WhatsApp as well.
So we are going to discuss about the analytics that happens on the platform, post a chat conversation
is over. Can you actually walk me through why this is important for business?
So as of today we have deployed over 100 plus chatbots and we generate a lot of data around
these chatbots. We process over 40 to 50 million messages a month and we've stored around 3 billion
different messages on our data stores. So all of this data is there and we wanted to make sense
out of this data and we also wanted to get some insights into the business. The other part was
that we all this data was stored in multiple places so we wanted to get all of this data into one common
place and lastly one challenge that we are facing was how do we feed this data into a machine learning
pipeline to make our bots smarter. Absolutely. So I believe we've got the architecture on the board,
we've got two streams. Can you just walk us through what we have on the board?
So the diagram shown on the board basically depicts two different pipelines. One is our real-time pipeline
which is on the bottom and above is an archival or historical based pipeline that we use to store
years and years of data. Okay. And so how does the real-time pipeline work?
So just to give you a context around how this pipeline gets triggered, on completion of chats
on each of these interfaces or channels as I mentioned, we gather a lot of metadata around
the conversation that happened on the platform. Once we have that data, we push that data into Kinesis.
So Kinesis acts as a data stream for us and just let's discuss about the real-time pipeline here.
So once the data is in Kinesis, Logstash pulls this data and throws this data to Elasticsearch.
Before throwing this data onto Elasticsearch, we do some computation and some manipulation of data on Logstash
on Logstash. And basis that, we push this data onto different indices on Elasticsearch. We chose Elasticsearch
because it was highly scalable out of the box and it was highly available. We've deployed this cluster
over multiple availability zones. So the data is always available out there. Finally, once the data is in
Elasticsearch in different indices, we fetch that data on our custom dashboard that we built in-house.
So you're using managed Elasticsearch as a service and you get a dashboard called Kibana built into it,
but you've still gone for a custom dashboard. Can you explain why did you take that choice?
So of course, Kibana works really well out of the box and when we were also building the data lake,
initially we started with Kibana. But what we realized was this dashboard we want to kind of dedicate to
a bot platform and we wanted to show the key metrics in the best possible manner. We wanted to build
some custom graphs around the bots and see how these bots are performing. So some of the key metrics
that are available in the dashboard are what are the types of messages the users are sending, what has been
the user journey on the bot, and is the bot being able to understand what the user says. So these were
the initial metrics, initial things that we thought about while building the custom dashboard.
Finally, what led to us to build this custom dashboard was the reason that we wanted to provide
these dashboards to the end customers or clients so that they could go back, log into the dashboard
securely and can see how their bots are performing in real time. So this is not just in-house but our
clients also get access to this dashboard where they can see is the bot working for their business or not.
That's brilliant. Now that you've got a real-time processing stream here, I wonder why you need a
batch processing engine. Can you walk us through it please?
As I mentioned earlier, we wanted to store data for years and years and we wanted this data to be
available to us anytime. If we were to look at a conversion that happened one year ago, we want
that data to be available on the platform. So how this particular pipeline works is, once the event is
in Kinesis, it triggers a lambda function. Lambda function when it gets triggered, it processes the data
that is coming into it from Kinesis and finally stores that data onto S3.
Uh-huh. And I see you've got Glue and Athena here as well. Can you walk us through the role that each
of these play in the architecture? Like I mentioned, all the data is now on S3 and we want to query it.
Uh-huh. Right? So how Glue comes into play is Glue helps us get the schema of the data
which can now be used on Amazon Athena and we can get an output of whatever data we want to read
around the chatbots. For example, if you were to go one year back and see on a particular day how many
conversations happened, right? So we can easily go on Athena and because Glue already has the schema
ready for us, we can write simple MySQL queries and get the results.
So that's a brilliant use of Glue where you use Glue to create the metadata, the structure around data,
that's brilliant. So this is fantastic. So where does Haptic go from here in terms of its architecture?
So we have a few improvements in mind. We want to move a few components which we manage on our own
to manage services like instead of Logstash we want to move to Amazon Firehose and for analytics also
we want to try out some other AWS services which are available out there. Second improvement we want to
do is that right now to view historical data and real-time data there are two different dashboards.
Mm-hmm. So we want to merge them and we want to see all this data in a common single dashboard.
Lastly, one of the major improvements that you want to do is we want to pull all of this data
that we are generating around the chatbots and you want to push this data into our machine learning
pipelines to make the bot smarter in real-time. That's brilliant. Thanks for walking us through your
architecture. Really appreciate it. Thanks for coming down running. And thanks for watching this
episode of This is My Architecture. See you around.
